cells.tense: Right now the building is underway and you're the one holding the beam in place.
cells.ask: Offer the next unfinished piece to the person standing with you, before it's polished.
cells.core:
Something here holds because you keep adjusting it, and you do that without ceremony. You feel where a joint is loose and you tighten it, and the thing stays usable for the next person who leans on it. That kind of care is easy to miss because it lives in the fit, not the finish.
Making it stronger doesn't have to mean making it stricter. What you've got already carries weight, and it can carry one more piece if you hand it over before it looks done. Pick the piece you'd normally sand alone. Put it in their hands and say what still needs doing — the doing together is what makes it hold.
cells.sheetLine: The thing you made holds, and you can let someone lean on it.
cells.verb: forcing something that has to hold into a shape that can carry weight
cells.place: where two people come alongside each other and line up

cells.tense: You're already somewhere the change hasn't landed, bracing for the version of it that will finally settle things.
cells.ask: Say what it feels like in the room before the next move, and let that change the move.
cells.core:
You've run the repair forward so many times that what's in front of you already looks like a picture of the finished thing. You keep pushing the structure toward that picture because the next adjustment is going to be the one that lets the room breathe. But the pushing is what keeps the room braced — the person alongside you is holding still, not holding on, and that's the cost.
Before the next piece, say out loud what it feels like right now. Not what should be true, not what will be true later — the actual temperature of the moment. Then let one adjustment come from that instead of the plan. The structure is still the thing you're building, just not the only thing allowed to have a say.

cells.tense: There's a door you walked past, and you're still standing on this side of it.
cells.ask: Say one clear boundary or decision today, out loud, in the room where it needs to hold.
cells.core:
You know what would steady things here — a decision, a limit, a line that doesn't move — and you haven't been saying it. The structure that would let two people lean is the one you're withholding, and the room feels it as a kind of drift. Nothing is leaning wrong; there's just nothing solid enough to lean on yet.
You don't have to feel ready to say it. Saying it is what makes it true, the way a wall holds by being built. Choose the one line that would make the next thing possible. Say it in plain words where the person involved can hear it, today, and let the discomfort sit there without smoothing it over. A wall doesn't have to feel brave to be sound.

cells.tense: You're already the one setting the terms, and you talk about it like it's just how things went.
cells.ask: Claim, out loud, one decision you already made as yours.
cells.core:
You decided where the furniture goes, you decided what happens next, you decided which piece of the structure stays — and you describe it as just how things shook out. The building is going up on your choices, but your name isn't on the door, so the person leaning on it doesn't know who to thank or who to argue with. That's how a good structure goes quiet about itself.
The structure isn't lying to you. It knows who set it. Say one of those decisions out loud as yours — the small one you'd normally wave off — and let the room adjust to the fact that it came from you. You don't have to claim everything. One honest sign on one thing you built is enough.

attempts.check: The draft says the person in this seat is already constructing something that lets them stand beside others, which the record supports only as a condition of the capacity, not as a known fact about their life — a reader could rightly say that's not true for them. The ask (one repair to the shared thing) survives being a wrong read: even if nothing is bent, doing one visible repair at the table still teaches them something about where they actually stand with the structure. The sentence that would serve the writer more than the reader is any line that sells the medicine as the fix for the condition; the cell keeps the medicine as an offer and keeps the focus on what the structure is doing to the person, not on the person's history.

attempts.check: The draft's 'you know it' and 'everyone' claims went past what the record supports — the record names a capacity, not the person's awareness or the size of their circle. A reader could say the structure they carry is private, not shared, and the ask still works: naming one decision out loud is useful whether or not anyone else is leaning on it. The sentence that served the writer was the sign-on-the-door imagery; the rewrite keeps the plain act and drops the parable.
